en: The location, the entry, the form, the target, and the characteristic itself;
the raising up, the awakening, and the resting of the wheel;
the arrival at the ground, and likewise the final state.
Repose, transformation, and likewise departure—
this thirteenfold supreme Śākta consciousness was indicated by Śambhu himself in all the Trika scriptures. (SomSv 2–3)
Five finger-breadths below the navel and two finger-breadths above the penis,
in the middle of that, is what is known as the place of the *cakra* called the *kanda*.
By means of the restraint of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, one should fix the mind right there.
Having mastered the movement of the breath correctly, one should lead it as far as the central point.
This is called "entry"; now I shall describe the form [of the wheel]:
the wheel resembles a triangle (śṛṅgāṭaka), and another is fixed with six spokes.
The bulb is like the color of a pomegranate flower, indeed red as a jasmine;
this form is declared to be the third, consisting of contemplation.
One should fix the mind in its center until it becomes steady there.
When the wind has been restrained and released, then one should point out the target (*lakṣa*).
Located in the center of the *kanda*-cakra is the digit (*kalā*) consisting of the Unstruck Sound (*anāhata*),
joined with lines above and below, and having the coiled form of a serpent.
The state situated above and below consists of both the sun and the moon;
that reality shines forth brilliantly, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns.
One should gaze upon that very Śakti for a moment with the practice of *kumbhaka* (retention).

This has been taught as the characteristic; hereafter follows the rite of raising [the breath]. One should recite the mantra with the movement of the *juṣat* exhalation, and one should contemplate the Supreme Goddess Śakti as awakened, like a staff.

Having risen from the center of the foundation and taken recourse to the path of the Suṣumṇā, it is called "raising" (utthāpana); thereafter, likewise, is "awakening" (bodhana). Residing in the bulb (kanda), one should pierce the navel; then, residing in the heart, the Grandfather (pitāmaha).
Having awakened Acyuta residing in the throat, Rudra directly situated at the base of the palate,
Īśa located between the eyebrows, and Sadāśiva at the door of Brahman,
one shall quickly proceed to the auspicious state that is beyond all support.
This is taught as the awakening; thereafter follows the resting of the wheel.
It is the natural petal, radiant, fluid, and like the stable sky.
It is the nectar, the crest, as well as Śakti and Brahmā.
Thus, the twelve wheels along with the *bindu* and *nāda* have indeed been described.
Piercing each wheel in succession, the Power (*śakti*) should rest at every moment within each wheel;
that Great Goddess rests there—this is the supreme resting in the wheels (*cakraviśrāma*).
First the heart trembles, as does the gateway of the palate;
his head whirls, which is the characteristic sign of the transfer of vision.
It causes each individual limb to whirl within the joints of the major and minor limbs.
And his heart trembles through the power of the perfect knowledge.
Whatever transformations and states the Being undergoes, one should not fear them; the Supreme Goddess is playing.
This very [power], intoxicated by the nectar, produces many transformations;
it shakes off the impure bonds arising from the supreme power— the transformations of the three impurities caused by what was done over many births.
The attainment of the stages has been described; now the state at the end is likewise declared.
At the time of the transition (saṃkrānti), there is horripilation, the shedding of tears, the onset of yawning, faltering speech, and internal sounds;
the bursting of knots, divine joy upon touch, and the vibrations of the *bindu* flash forth from the root of the navel.
The final state has been fully described; now, however, the state of rest is being explained:
when the power (śakti) emerging from the navel-center (nābhicakra) awakens, then everything situated externally within the collection of sense organs has set.
When that supreme power is perfectly dissolved into the highest state,
then the subject perceives no other object whatsoever;
when the power rests within Śiva, that is called "rest."
Wherever there is rest for power, there the mind should go to dissolution;
then the Self must be known as the Supreme Self by those of certain realization.
Having become Śiva, the Self is indeed that very transformation.
It always rains down divine nectar that sustains living beings. By fixing the mind there, she—the goddess—shall enter once again;
thus, the arrival [of the breath] is correctly described as the thirteenth.
